newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seeks prosecutions in bond fraud.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seeks prosecutions in bond fraud.

text.p: The Brazilian Senate Wednesday wrapped up a probe of a multi-million dollar municipal bond fraud, recommending that prosecutors consider criminal proceedings against a host of officials.

A Senate official said a Congressional Committee of Inquiry (CPI) had found evidence that state officials and bond traders colluded to siphon off more than 220 million reais (about $200 million) from the scam.
"The CPI found that more than 220 million reais was siphoned off through fraudulent trades and contracts," said the official, who acted as an investigator for the committee.
The committee spent six months investigating allegations that some states and municipalities sold debt at far below its market value to friendly brokerages.
The brokers then sold the securities to others involved in the scheme until the debt ended up in the hands of state pension funds and some large private banks.
The illicit profits allegedly made their way to secret bank accounts in Paraguay and the Caribbean.

The probe named as the chief culprits an official at South America's largest private bank, Bradesco, the owners of a host of small broking houses and banks and a former finance executive of Sao Paulo city.

"Bradesco provided testimony to the CPI on state bonds and is calm with regard to the outcome because it acted within the rules of the market. The same applies to the testimony of its officials," a spokeswoman said.
The senators also assigned a degree of blame to former Sao Paulo mayor and presidential hopeful Paulo Maluf and his successor Celso Pitta.

Three of Brazil's 27 states were found to have been involved in the debt scam -- Alagoas, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina -- and three municipalities, all in Sao Paulo state -- Sao Paulo, Osasco and Guarulhos.
"It is now up to the public prosecutors to bring criminal charges and possibly civil charges so the monies can be recovered," the Senate official said.
A judge in Sao Paulo, Joao Carlos da Rocha Matos, has already begun studying the case.
